pathway.title: Web Development
pathway.description: A progressive pathway for planning, building, testing, securing and operating modern websites and web applications.

course.title: Web Development — Advanced
course.minimum_runtime_version: Modern evergreen browser and Node.js 20+ for tooling
course.dependencies: Standards-based browser APIs; optional tooling must be documented and version-pinned.
course.short_description: Architect, secure, optimize, deploy and observe production-oriented web applications across front-end and back-end boundaries.
course.prerequisites: Completion of Web Development — Intermediate or equivalent experience with component-based interfaces, JavaScript modules, APIs, state, routing, testing and build tooling.
learning_outcomes: Design full-stack web architectures with clear trust and data boundaries.
Implement authentication concepts, authorization checks and secure session practices.
Optimize performance, accessibility, reliability and resilience using measurements.
Deploy and observe production-oriented applications with automated quality controls.

topics.title: Application architecture and rendering strategies
topics.description: A guided lesson about application architecture and rendering strategies with examples and practical application.

lesson.title: Application architecture and rendering strategies
objectives: Explain the core ideas behind application architecture and rendering strategies.
Apply application architecture and rendering strategies in a small, testable web-development task.
Evaluate accessibility, security or maintainability implications relevant to application architecture and rendering strategies.

blocks.title: Concepts and engineering context
blocks.body:
Production web engineering is a systems discipline. A browser interface, application server, identity provider, database, cache, object storage and delivery network form a system with different trust boundaries and failure modes. Architecture must make those boundaries explicit: the browser is controlled by the user, so client-side checks improve usability but cannot enforce authorization. The server must authenticate requests, authorize every protected action, validate inputs, constrain resource use and return only data the caller may access. Authentication establishes identity; authorization evaluates permission for a particular resource and operation. Session design must account for cookie flags, CSRF defenses, token exposure, expiration and revocation. Performance work should begin with field or laboratory measurements and a clear user impact, not premature micro-optimization. Reliability requires timeouts, bounded retries, idempotency where appropriate, graceful degradation and useful observability without logging secrets or sensitive payloads. Deployment is repeatable when builds, migrations, tests, environment configuration and rollback procedures are documented and automated. Accessibility, privacy and security are architectural requirements, not a final styling pass. The capstone should demonstrate these decisions with evidence, threat modelling, tests, operational notes and explicit limitations rather than claiming that a classroom prototype is production-certified.

In this lesson, focus specifically on application architecture and rendering strategies. Start by stating the user need and the expected behavior. Identify the browser or server responsibility involved, then select the smallest standards-based tool that solves the problem. Work through one normal case and at least one boundary case. Inspect the result in developer tools, explain why the implementation behaves as it does, and record assumptions that would need verification in a real deployment. Avoid copying a framework pattern without understanding the browser or HTTP behavior underneath it.

blocks.title: A small executable example
blocks.expected_output: Learning Web Development: HTML, CSS, JavaScript
blocks.explanation: This small JavaScript example models data and transforms it into a readable summary. It runs in Node.js and demonstrates the language behavior used in browser scripts; the surrounding lesson explains how the same idea fits into web architecture.

blocks.title: How the parts relate

blocks.content: User goal → Browser client → authenticated API boundary → domain service → persistence

blocks.title: Guided practical activity
instructions: Create a small demonstration of application architecture and rendering strategies. Write down the expected behavior before coding, implement it with semantic and standards-based web technologies, then test a normal case, a boundary case and keyboard-only use. Explain one trade-off in your design.
success_checks: The result meets the stated behavior and has a clear structure.
A normal and a boundary or failure case are checked.
The learner can explain the diagram and one design trade-off.

blocks.title: Concepts and engineering context
blocks.body:
Production web engineering is a systems discipline. A browser interface, application server, identity provider, database, cache, object storage and delivery network form a system with different trust boundaries and failure modes. Architecture must make those boundaries explicit: the browser is controlled by the user, so client-side checks improve usability but cannot enforce authorization. The server must authenticate requests, authorize every protected action, validate inputs, constrain resource use and return only data the caller may access. Authentication establishes identity; authorization evaluates permission for a particular resource and operation. Session design must account for cookie flags, CSRF defenses, token exposure, expiration and revocation. Performance work should begin with field or laboratory measurements and a clear user impact, not premature micro-optimization. Reliability requires timeouts, bounded retries, idempotency where appropriate, graceful degradation and useful observability without logging secrets or sensitive payloads. Deployment is repeatable when builds, migrations, tests, environment configuration and rollback procedures are documented and automated. Accessibility, privacy and security are architectural requirements, not a final styling pass. The capstone should demonstrate these decisions with evidence, threat modelling, tests, operational notes and explicit limitations rather than claiming that a classroom prototype is production-certified.

In this lesson, focus specifically on accessibility engineering and internationalization. Start by stating the user need and the expected behavior. Identify the browser or server responsibility involved, then select the smallest standards-based tool that solves the problem. Work through one normal case and at least one boundary case. Inspect the result in developer tools, explain why the implementation behaves as it does, and record assumptions that would need verification in a real deployment. Avoid copying a framework pattern without understanding the browser or HTTP behavior underneath it.

practical_project.title: Web Development — Advanced Capstone
practical_project.purpose: Design and build a production-oriented full-stack web application prototype that demonstrates the course outcomes.
privacy_and_limits: Use fictional data and test accounts only; do not connect to Marian production systems or real learner records.
Do not put credentials, API secrets or private keys in browser code.
A learning prototype is not a security certification or production approval.
requirements: Write a short user and feature brief with acceptance criteria.
Use semantic HTML, responsive CSS and a clear component or page structure.
Implement the required interactions and validate user input.
Handle empty, loading, success and error states where data is asynchronous.
Include keyboard and accessibility checks appropriate to the interface.
Add automated tests for important behavior and document setup and limitations.
suggested_steps: Define users, scope, acceptance criteria and a simple architecture diagram.
Build the semantic structure and responsive visual system.
Implement behavior and data boundaries in small increments.
Test normal, boundary, accessibility and failure cases.
Review performance, security and maintainability appropriate to the level.
Document setup, screenshots, decisions and known limitations.
success_checks: The application satisfies its stated acceptance criteria.
The interface works at mobile and desktop widths.
Core tasks are possible using a keyboard.
Important normal and failure cases are tested.
The README explains setup, architecture and limitations.

rubric.look_for: Clear scope, coherent structure and justified design decisions.
Correct behavior, readable code and maintainable organization.
Semantic structure, keyboard use, contrast and adaptable layout.
Relevant automated and manual tests, including boundary cases.
Reproducible setup, diagrams, trade-offs and honest limitations.
